summary: COSE (RFC 9052) has no direct way to use hash algorithms, but hashes are needed in places such as indirect signatures, where the hash of content is signed, and when identifying a certificate by its fingerprint. This document defines hash algorithms that are identified by COSE algorithm identifiers.

plainLanguage.summary: A hash is like a short fingerprint of a long document. This document gives the COSE system names for several fingerprint recipes so messages can say which one they used.

questions: how to identify a certificate by hash in cose
what hash algorithms does cose support
how do i use sha-256 in cose
subtitle: Naming and using standard hash functions in signed and encrypted messages.

tldr.problem: COSE (CBOR Object Signing and Encryption) has no standard way to identify which hash algorithm was used when hashing content for signatures or object identification.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9054 assigns COSE algorithm identifiers to standard hash functions—SHA-1, SHA-2 variants (SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512, and truncated forms), and SHAKE-128 and SHAKE-256—so messages can declare which hash they use.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now use hash functions with COSE in two common scenarios: indirect signatures (where the hash of content is signed rather than the content itself) and identifying objects by their hash fingerprint.

today: RFC 9054 is an Informational document published in August 2022 and remains the standard way to use hash algorithms with COSE. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
COSE (RFC 9052) is a way to sign and encrypt messages using the CBOR format. While COSE defines many security algorithms, it does not directly specify how to use hash functions—but hashes are crucial in two important scenarios.

Indirect signing is useful when the content is very large. Instead of signing the entire content, the sender hashes it, signs the hash, and sends both the hash and the signature. The receiver can then validate the signature on the hash without downloading all the content first. This is especially valuable in constrained environments where devices have limited memory.

Object identification happens when you want to find or verify a certificate or other object by its hash fingerprint. For example, a message might say 'look for the certificate with this hash value' rather than including the whole certificate.
sections.plainLanguage: When you want to sign something huge, you can just sign a short fingerprint instead. When you want to find a certificate, you can ask for the one that matches a specific fingerprint. This document lists the fingerprints COSE can use.

sections.title: Using Hash Functions Safely
sections.content:
Hash functions are everywhere in cryptography, but they are not all equally safe. A collision attack is when someone finds two different inputs that hash to the same value—a serious problem for security-critical uses.

Some hash functions are suitable only for non-cryptographic purposes. SHA-1, for instance, has known collision attacks and the IETF discouraged its use in RFC 6194. Yet it may still be needed for legacy systems that only support SHA-1. When used for filtering (finding candidates that might be correct), SHA-1 is acceptable because you verify the result afterward. When used for signing, it should be avoided.

The RFC divides hash functions into two categories: those approved for cryptographic use (like SHA-256) and those approved for filtering only (like SHA-1). Applications must carefully choose a hash based on how it will be used.
sections.plainLanguage: Some fingerprints are really strong and hard to fake, while others are old and weak. The trick is knowing which to use when. If you just need a hint to find something, a weak fingerprint is okay. But if you are signing something important, use a strong one.

sections.title: The Hash Algorithms
sections.content:
RFC 9054 registers the following hash algorithms with COSE algorithm identifiers.

SHA-1 (algorithm -14) produces a 160-bit hash. As mentioned, it has known collision attacks and is approved for filtering only, not for cryptographic purposes.

SHA-256/64 (algorithm -15) is SHA-256 truncated to 64 bits. It reduces transmission size but increases collision risk. It is approved for filtering only.

SHA-256 (algorithm -16) is the most common 256-bit hash today. It is efficient on 32-bit hardware and approved for full cryptographic use.

SHA-384 (algorithm -43) and SHA-512 (algorithm -44) are the 64-bit versions, efficient on modern processors, and approved for cryptographic use.

SHA-512/256 (algorithm -17) runs as efficiently as SHA-512 but delivers only 256 bits of output, matching SHA-256's security level while benefiting from 64-bit hardware optimization.

SHAKE-128 (algorithm -18) and SHAKE-256 (algorithm -45) are extendable-output functions from the SHA-3 family. SHAKE-128 produces 256 bits by default, and SHAKE-256 produces 512 bits. Both are approved for cryptographic use.
sections.plainLanguage: There are different recipes for making fingerprints, each with a name and a number. Some are old and weak, some are new and strong. You pick the one that fits your needs.

sections.title: Security Concerns
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that applications must understand what properties of a hash function they actually need. Collision resistance (finding two messages with the same hash) matters for cryptographic uses but not for simple filtering. Preimage resistance (finding a message that hashes to a given value) matters only sometimes.

Longer hash values are generally stronger than shorter ones, but transmission size and timeliness matter too. The choice of hash length is a trade-off.

Most importantly, cryptographic strength weakens over time as new attacks are discovered. Applications should design with algorithm agility in mind—the ability to switch to a stronger hash function if the current one shows signs of weakness.
sections.plainLanguage: Hash functions can get weaker as people find new tricks to break them. So build your system so you can swap in a stronger one when needed, rather than baking in one forever.
